h1: Straight bourbon and bottled in bond
title: Straight Bourbon and Bottled in Bond | Craft Beer School
desc: What straight bourbon and bottled in bond mean on an American whiskey label, the legal rules behind each and what they tell you about the glass.
teaser: Two phrases on a bourbon label carry real legal weight. Most marketing words do not.
standfirst: American whiskey labels are crowded with words. Two of them, straight and bottled in bond, are defined in US federal rules and tell you something concrete about age and strength. Here is how to read them.
sections: Start with what makes a bourbon

Bourbon has to meet a set of US federal rules before any other word on the label matters. It must be made in the United States from a mash of at least 51% corn. It must be distilled to no more than 80% ABV (160 proof), go into the barrel at no more than 62.5% ABV (125 proof) and be matured in new charred oak containers. It must be bottled at no less than 40% ABV (80 proof). Nothing may be added apart from water.

Notice what is missing: a minimum age. Plain bourbon can, in principle, spend a very short time in the barrel. That is the gap the word straight fills. Our guide to bourbon mash bills covers the grain side.
Straight means at least two years

Straight bourbon must meet all the bourbon rules and be aged for at least two years in new charred oak. If it is under four years old, the label must state its age. So a straight bourbon with no age statement is at least four years old.

Straight bourbon also cannot contain added colouring or flavouring. If it is a blend of straight bourbons, they must all come from the same state. That is why you may see a state name such as Kentucky or Tennessee next to the word straight.

The two year rule is short by Scotch standards, where three years is the floor for any whisky. But new charred oak gives flavour much faster than the refill casks used for most Scotch. The hot summers in Kentucky push spirit in and out of the wood quickly. A four year old bourbon can taste far more of oak than a four year old Scotch.
Bottled in bond is a law from 1897

The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 was one of the first consumer protection laws in the United States. At the time, some sellers stretched whiskey with neutral spirit, colouring and flavourings. The Act gave honest producers a way to prove what was in the bottle, with the government acting as guarantor.

To carry the words bottled in bond, an American spirit must be:

  • The product of one distilling season, either January to June or July to December, by one distiller at one distillery.
  • Aged at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse under government supervision.
  • Bottled at exactly 100 proof, which is 50% ABV.
  • Labelled with the distillery where it was made and, if different, where it was bottled.

Bottled in bond is not limited to bourbon. Rye, apple brandy and other spirits can carry it too, as long as they meet the rules.
What each term tells you in the glass

Straight tells you about age and purity: two years minimum, no colouring, no flavouring. Bottled in bond tells you more. You know the whiskey is at least four years old, came from one distillery in one season and is at 50% ABV.

That 50% ABV matters when you taste. A bottled in bond bourbon will feel hotter and richer than a typical 40% bourbon. Add a few drops of water and the vanilla, caramel and baking spice often open up. Our guide to tasting past the alcohol burn is worth reading before you pour one neat.

Neither term promises quality. A four year old bottled in bond whiskey can be thin or brilliant. They are transparency labels, not medals.
Words that sound legal but are not

Other common bourbon label phrases have no strict federal definition. Small batch, reserve, single barrel, hand crafted and special select are largely the producer's own claims. Some producers use them carefully. Some do not. Our guide to what small batch means looks at one of them closely.

A useful habit is to sort every phrase on a label into defined and undefined. Bourbon, straight, bottled in bond and an age statement are defined. Almost everything else is marketing until the producer tells you more.

Imported bourbon reaches Indian shelves through state excise systems, so availability and price vary a great deal from state to state. Bottled in bond bourbons are less common than standard expressions. Duty free and specialist stores in the metros are the likeliest places to find them.

In Indian heat, store any bottle upright, away from sunlight, in the coolest cupboard you have. A higher strength bourbon is no more fragile than a 40% one. Once opened, the air in the bottle slowly changes the aroma, which our guide to storing an opened bottle explains.
Compare a straight and a bonded bourbon

Your first step: taste a standard straight bourbon next to a bottled in bond one, 20 ml each, in tulip glasses. Nose both neat. Then bring the bonded one down with water until it smells about as strong as the other. What is left once the strength is matched is the difference in age, wood and distillery. Drink water between sips and never drink and drive.
faqs: At least two years. If it is under four years old, the label must state the age.
What proof is bottled in bond whiskey?
Is bottled in bond better than straight bourbon?
Not necessarily. It guarantees one distillery, one season, at least four years and 50% ABV, but it does not guarantee flavour.
Does small batch have a legal meaning?
No. Small batch has no federal definition in the United States. It is the producer's own description.
